concept: OTPFlow is the whole one-time-code step of a sign-in, drawn as one small appliance: a title, one display window that says where the code went and how long until a new one may be asked for, the row of digit windows, and a plain key to send again. The window reads out the state and the key only acts.

default_to_avoid.pattern: otp flow as a centred card with a resend link that carries its countdown in brackets and a big accent verify button
default_to_avoid.why_not: The countdown is repeated in the link and the accent is spent on a button the finished code does not need; here the window holds the countdown once and the code verifies itself when the last digit lands.

default_to_avoid.pattern: otp flow that shakes the boxes and turns them green or red on a verdict
default_to_avoid.why_not: It tells the verdict by colour and motion alone; here the verdict is a glyph and words, read out through the status line.

references.source: Braun ET 66 calculator (Dietrich Lubs, 1987): one window carries the reading and the keys below only act
Braun T 1000 world receiver (Dieter Rams, 1963): the dial scale is read at the top of the case, the controls sit under it
system/FORM.md display and input classes: recessed window, printing on the inset line
WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: status role for a polite live region that does not take focus

derivation.consequence: the display window sits at the top of the unit
derivation.form: The window with the destination and the countdown comes straight after the title, above the digit row.

derivation.consequence: the window is recessed into the body (inverse light)
derivation.form: The window takes surface.sunken and elevation.well, the same cut-in as the digit cells, so the reading never looks like a key.

derivation.consequence: the display is a live region (polite) and never a control
derivation.form: A status line is a polite live region that speaks the verdicts and the moment a new code may be asked for, and the ticking seconds stay silent.

derivation.consequence: tabular figures everywhere a number changes
derivation.form: The countdown and the destination use tabular figures, so the seconds change without the window width moving.

derivation.consequence: fixed positions, so a unit's layout does not reflow between states
derivation.form: The message line keeps one line of height whether it holds a hint, the success words or nothing.

derivation.consequence: orange appears once per unit, on the primary control's body only
derivation.form: The send-again key is a plain key and every part of the flow is ink; the one orange part is left to the host unit.

options.name: plain stack with the countdown in the key
display window with destination and countdown

variants.reason: B puts the destination and the countdown in one recessed window so the state is read once at the top, and the key only acts; A repeats the countdown in a disabled key and spends the sentence on the destination, and C prints a three-word legend for a path that has no choices, which breaks the legend rule that a legend lists options.

root.why: The step stacks title, window, digit row, message and key in one column on the body's inset line, and its blocks keep their places between states.

title.why: The step's name is the unit's heading in medium weight, sentence case, printed on the inset line above the window.

window.why: One recessed window says where the code went on its start side and how long until a new one on its end side, in the inverse light of the digit cells.

sent.why: The small word that names the destination is caption size in secondary ink, so the number below it is read first.

destination.why: The phone number or address is printed in medium weight with tabular figures and wraps anywhere, so a long address never pushes the countdown out of the window.

reading.why: The countdown is a minutes-and-seconds reading in tabular figures, hidden from assistive tech because the status line speaks it only when it ends.

field.why: The digit row is the PinInput as it is, with its own label and 44px cells; the flow adds nothing around it but the same gap as the other blocks.

line.why: The message line under the digits holds a hint or the success words and keeps one line of height so nothing below it jumps.

mark.why: A check glyph stands before the success words, so the verdict is a mark and words and never a colour.

actions.why: The send-again key stands on its own row on the inset line, a 44px key as large as every key in dial.

resend.why: The resend key is a plain body-coloured key with no orange, because the orange belongs to the host unit's one primary control.

data-ready.why: When the countdown ends the reading goes from secondary to primary ink and the key rises from its flat, disabled height, so the change is a height as well as a tone.

data-status=success.why: After a good code the digits stop taking input, a check and the words print under them in primary ink, and the key goes flat.

data-status=verifying.why: While the host checks the code the digits are read-only, the key is flat and the words go to primary ink, so a second press or a changed digit cannot cross a check in flight.

@media forced-colors: active.why: In forced colours the window keeps a real border and its text and the success glyph draw in the system text colour.
